# Passenger journeys hit record high but revenue lags 

- By Rich Wilcock
- |
- 19 June 2026
- News

 Office of Rail and Road 

However, punctuality has continued to fall with 66% of trains arriving on time last year (defined as arriving within 59 seconds of their scheduled time).

According to annual data released by the Office of Rail and Road (ORR), passengers made 1.83 billion journeys between April 2025 and March 2026. This figure marks the highest volume of rail usage recorded across the network since 1920.

However, punctuality has continued to fall with 66% of trains arriving on time last year (defined as arriving within 59 seconds of their scheduled time).

According to annual data released by the Office of Rail and Road (ORR), passengers made 1.83 billion journeys between April 2025 and March 2026. This figure marks the highest volume of rail usage recorded across the network since 1920.

The results comfortably clear the modern, pre-COVID high of 1.75 billion journeys set in 2018–19, representing a 6% year-on-year growth against the 1.73 billion recorded last year.

Unsurprisingly, the Elizabeth Line contributed considerably to the figures boost with 257 million journeys made on the line last year. In the last quarter recorded, from January – March 2026, it recorded a further 4% increase on the same period last year.

The data also paints a clear picture of a demand for leisure and flexible travel amongst passengers with off-peak journeys recording a strong 6% annual rise, climbing from 799 million to 844 million.

Conversely, this came at the cost of the typical weekday daily commute. Despite recording a 4% annual bump to 234 million, it is still considerably down on the pre-pandemic peak of 588 million annual journeys.

This has had an inevitable impact on revenues with total revenue standing at £12.3 billion, still just over a billion pounds short of the £13.4 billion generated before the pandemic.

The fall in punctuality alongside the rise in passengers returning to the railway led ORR to warn that the industry must ensure the gap between the two figures does not get any larger.

"It's great news that more people are using the railway," said Graham Richards, Director of Planning and Performance at the ORR. "The Elizabeth line has been a massive boost to rail, but behind the usage figures there is a significant shift to how and when we use the rail network."

Richards added, “As more people are using the railway it's important to have a relentless focus in ensuring trains are punctual and reliable as possible.” 

ORR also warned that the rise in spilt ticketing could be having an effect on the number of journeys made. In the report, it said: “Rail Delivery Group (RDG) estimates that overall, around 5% of passenger journeys between April 2023 and March 2024 were made using split tickets (it was around 4% in the previous year).

“Split ticketing has become more prevalent in recent years, therefore the extent to which it affects rail usage statistics has increased. It may be that the recovery of journeys relative to before the pandemic is overstated.”

In the last quarter, all but four operators saw growth, with East Coast Main Line (ECML) operators all the worst affected – LNER, Caledonian Sleeper and open access operators Hull Trains and Grand Central all recorded a fall in passenger numbers between January and March, compared to the same quarter last year.

Railway Industry Association (RIA) Chief Executive Darren Caplan said: “The news from the ORR that passenger numbers are at record levels is no surprise and backs up what we at the Railway Industry Association have been saying for several years now, in terms of the post-Covid return to rail.

The present DfT figures support the ORR's report too, showing current passenger numbers at around 110% of pre-Covid levels including the Elizabeth line, and 100% if not included.

We will clearly need more capacity in the future, and plan for consistently growing numbers of rail users, both passengers and freight.”
